D.2 Potential Extensions
We discuss here a few potential extensions of the IO-aware approach to speed up deep learning training.
Multi-GPU Attention.Large language models are trained on hundreds or thousands of GPUs, and
one typically splits the attention computation between 4-8 GPUs on the same node [77]. This introduces
another level of memory hierarchy: beside GPU SRAM and GPU HBM, we also have the HBM of other
25

title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
text:
GPUs. For very long sequences, the diﬀerent GPUs on the same node can cooperate to compute attention by
taking into account the asymmetry of diﬀerent levels of memory hierarchy.
Sparse MLP layers.Typical dense MLP layers are compute-bound and not memory-bound. To improve
their eﬃciency, MLP layers with sparse weight matrices can be used [17]. However, many sparse MLP layers
are instead memory-bound, and their speedup is often not proportional to the sparsity. We believe that an
IO-aware implementation can alleviate this issue and realize the beneﬁts of sparsity. We are excited about
future work in this direction, to reduce the computational requirement of large models and improve their
wall-block runtime.
Kernel machine learning. Our approach in FlashAttention relies on the fact that the𝑁𝑁
attention matrix is a function of a low-rank matrixQK> (of rank𝑑 𝑁). As a result, we can repeatedly
load the inputsQ K and recompute the block of the attention matrix that we need, signiﬁcantly reducing
HBM access. As similar scenario happens in kernel machine learning: each element𝐾𝑖𝑗 of the𝑁𝑁 kernel
matrix K is a function of two vectors of size𝑑𝑁, as it measures the similarity between two datapoints𝑥𝑖
and𝑥𝑗. The KeOps library [8, 26] is a successful example of how reducing memory reads/writes can speed up
kernel operations. We hope that this will motivate kernel methods that focus more on reducing IOs instead
of just FLOPs.
E Full Experimental Results
E.1 BERT
We train BERT-large following the training procedure and hyperparameters of the reference MLPerf 1.1
implementation. In particular, we use the LAMB optimizer with learning rate 3.75e-3, with batch size 448,
trained for at most 7100 steps. The training is stopped once the validation accuracy (for masked language
modeling) reaches the target 72.0%, and the wall-clock run-time is measured. We train with FP16 precision
using Apex AMP (with O2 optimization level).
We compare our results with the reported training speed from Nvidia that was submitted to MLPerf 1.1
(Table 1).
We use the same train / validation data split provided by MLPerf 1.1 reference implementation. In
particular, we evaluate on the same 10000 validation examples as the baseline from Nvidia.
We train the model on 8A100-80GB GPUs. Each training run takes between 16 and 19 minutes, and we
average the results of 10 runs.

E.2 GPT-2
We use the standard implementations of GPT-2 [67] from Huggingface transformers library and from
Nvidia’s Megatron-LM repo. We follow the training recipe of the Megatron-LM repo.
We use an eﬀective batch size of 512, and use gradient accumulation to ﬁt into available GPU memory.
We use the AdamW optimizer, with learning rate 6e-4 for GPT-2 small and 1.5e-4 for GPT-2 medium, and
weight decay of 0.1. All models are trained with the same hyperparameters for 400K steps. We run all
implementations with mixed-precision training (PyTorch AMP).
We use the Openwebtext dataset, with the GPT-2 BPE tokenizer. We randomly select 0.5% of the dataset
as the validation set, with the rest being used as training set. This random selection of validation set is done
once, and all models are evaluated on the same validation set.
We train the model on 8A100-40GB GPUs, and we measure the wall-clock training time. Training
GPT-2 small takes between 2.7-9.5 days, and training GPT-2 medium takes between 6.9-21.0 days (Table 2).

E.3 LRA details
We follow the hyperparameters from the Long-range arena paper [80], the Long-range arena repo (https:
//github.com/google-research/long-range-arena), and the Nyströmformer reproduction [90]. To be
generous to the baseline methods, if we are unable to reproduce the performance of any baseline for any of
the ﬁve tasks, we report the better performance from Tay et al.[80] or Xiong et al.[90] for that baseline on
that task.
After hyperparameter tuning, almost all of the attention methods achieve similar accuracy on all of the
ﬁve LRA tasks.
We run all methods with mixed-precision training, except for Performer (not stable with mixed precision)
and Local Attention (implementation does not support FP16).
To calculate the overall wallclock-time speedup, we take the geometric mean of the wallclock-time speedup
of each of the ﬁve tasks.
Path-X For Path-X and Path-256, we follow the hyperparameters from the PathFinder-32 experiments
from the long-range arena paper[80]. For both, we ﬁrst pretrain a model on Path-64. We take the checkpoint
after 200 epochs, upsample its positional embedding (we duplicate the positional embeddings gridwise in
space), and ﬁne-tune it on the downstream task for 200 epochs with one epoch of linear warmup, and cosine
decay of the learning rate. For Path-X, we take the best performing checkpoint (according to val accuracy),
and additionally ﬁne-tune it for 200 epochs with the same warmup and learning rate (this adds roughly 4
points of accuracy toFlashAttention for Path-X, but the model starts overﬁtting afterwards).

E.6 Full Benchmarking Results
We report the full benchmarking results and experimental details on A100.
Baselines We compare against reference implementations for exact attention from PyTorch/HuggingFace
and Megatron, approximate attention, and sparse attention. For approximate attention, we compare against
reference implementations of Reformer [51], Local Attention [68], Linformer Attention [84], Smyrf [19], and
LongShortFormer (LSFormer) [94]. For sparse attention, we compare against reference implementations of
Block-Sparse Attention form OpenAI [11], Longformer[3], and BigBird Attention [92]. For the approximate
and sparse attention, we use a compression ratio of 1/8, or a compressed sequence length of 256, whichever is
smaller.
Setup We measure runtime and memory usage of the attention computation with 8 heads of dimension 64,
and batch size 16 on a machine with one A100 GPU with 40 GB of GPU HBM. We vary sequence length
in our experiments. We compute attention on random vectors forQ, K, and V (we do not measure the
projection from the hidden layer). For dropout, we use dropout 0.1; for masking, we use a padding mask
with uniformly-random mask lengths between the total sequence length and the total sequence length minus
20. To measure runtime, we take the average of 100 measurements of the attention call. We only measure
memory footprint once, since it does not vary between runs.

title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need
text:
L38: ###### Abstract
L39: Multi-head attention layers, as used in the Transformer neural sequence model, are a powerful alternative to RNNs for moving information across and between sequences. While training these layers is generally fast and simple, due to parallelizability across the length of the sequence, incremental inference (where such paralleization is impossible) is often slow, due to the memory-bandwidth cost of repeatedly loading the large "keys" and "values" tensors.
L40: We propose a variant called multi-query attention, where the keys and values are shared across all of the different attention "heads", greatly reducing the size of these tensors and hence the memory bandwidth requirements of incremental decoding. We verify experimentally that the resulting models can indeed be much faster to decode, and incur only minor quality degradation from the baseline.
L41: ## 1 Introduction
L42: The Transformer neural sequence model [cite23†Vaswani et al., 2017 ] has emerged as a popular alternative to recurrent sequence models. Transformer relies on attention layers to communicate information between and across sequences. One major challenge with Transformer is the speed of incremental inference.
L43: As we will discuss, the speed of incremental Transformer inference on modern computing hardware is limited by the memory bandwidth necessary to reload the large "keys" and "values" tensors which encode the state of the attention layers. In the following sections, we will review the multi-head-attention layers used by Transformer, provide a performance analysis, and propose an architectural variation (multi-query attention) which greatly improves inference speed with only minor quality degradation.

title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
text:
L42: ###### Abstract
L43: Multi-query attention (MQA), which only uses a single key-value head, drastically speeds up decoder inference. However, MQA can lead to quality degradation, and moreover it may not be desirable to train a separate model just for faster inference.
L44: We (1) propose a recipe for uptraining existing multi-head language model checkpoints into models with MQA using 5% of original pre-training compute, and (2) introduce grouped-query attention (GQA), a generalization of multi-query attention which uses an intermediate (more than one, less than number of query heads) number of key-value heads. We show that uptrained GQA achieves quality close to multi-head attention with comparable speed to MQA.
L45: ## 1 Introduction
L46: 
L47: Autoregressive decoder inference is a severe bottleneck for Transformer models due to the memory bandwidth overhead from loading decoder weights and all attention keys and values at every decoding step (cite27†Shazeer, 2019 ; cite28†Pope et al., 2022 ; cite29†de Jong et al., 2022 ). The memory bandwidth from loading keys and values can be sharply reduced through multi-query attention (cite27†Shazeer, 2019 ), which uses multiple query heads but single key and value heads.
L48: However, multi-query attention (MQA) can lead to quality degradation and training instability, and it may not be feasible to train separate models optimized for quality and inference. Moreover, while some language models already use multi-query attention, such as PaLM (cite30†Chowdhery et al., 2022 ), many do not, including publicly available language models such as T5 (cite31†Raffel et al., 2020 ) and LLaMA (cite32†Touvron et al., 2023 ).
L49: This work contains two contributions for faster inference with large language models. First, we show that language model checkpoints with multi-head attention (MHA) can be uptrained (cite33†Komatsuzaki et al., 2022 ) to use MQA with a small fraction of original training compute. This presents a cost-effective method to obtain fast multi-query as well as high-quality MHA checkpoints.

title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
text:
L50: Second, we propose grouped-query attention (GQA), an interpolation between multi-head and multi-query attention with single key and value heads per subgroup of query heads. We show that uptrained GQA achieves quality close to multi-head attention while being almost as fast as multi-query attention.
L51: ## 2 Method
L52: ### 2.1 Uptraining
L53: Generating a multi-query model from a multi-head model takes place in two steps: first, converting the checkpoint, and second, additional pre-training to allow the model to adapt to its new structure. Figure cite34†1 shows the process for converting a multi-head checkpoint into a multi-query checkpoint.
L54: The projection matrices for key and value heads are mean pooled into single projection matrices, which we find works better than selecting a single key and value head or randomly initializing new key and value heads from scratch.
L55: cite35†Image: Refer to caption Figure 1: Overview of conversion from multi-head to multi-query attention. Key and value projection matrices from all heads are mean pooled into a single head.
L56: 
L57: The converted checkpoint is then pre-trained for a small proportion $\alpha$ of its original training steps on the same pre-training recipe.
L58: ### 2.2 Grouped-query attention
L59: 
L60: cite36†Image: Refer to caption Figure 2: Overview of grouped-query method. Multi-head attention has H query, key, and value heads. Multi-query attention shares single key and value heads across all query heads. Grouped-query attention instead shares single key and value heads for each group of query heads, interpolating between multi-head and multi-query attention.
L61: Grouped-query attention divides query heads into $G$ groups, each of which shares a single key head and value head. GQA-g refers to grouped-query with $G$ groups. GQA-$1$, with a single group and therefore single key and value head, is equivalent to MQA, while GQA-h, with groups equal to number of heads, is equivalent to MHA. Figure cite37†2 shows a comparison of grouped-query attention and multi-head/multi-query attention.
L62: When converting a multi-head checkpoint to a GQA checkpoint, we construct each group key and value head by mean-pooling all the original heads within that group.

title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
text:
L62: When converting a multi-head checkpoint to a GQA checkpoint, we construct each group key and value head by mean-pooling all the original heads within that group.
L63: An intermediate number of groups leads to an interpolated model that is higher quality than MQA but faster than MHA, and, as we will show, represents a favorable trade-off. Going from MHA to MQA reduces $H$ key and value heads to a single key and value head, reducing the size of the key-value cache and therefore amount of data that needs to be loaded by a factor of $H$.
L64: However, larger models generally scale the number of heads, such that multi-query attention represents a more aggressive cut in both memory bandwidth and capacity. GQA lets us keep the same proportional decrease in bandwidth and capacity as model size increases.
L65: Moreover, larger models suffer relatively less from memory bandwidth overhead from attention, as the KV-cache scales with model dimension while model FLOPs and parameters scale with the square of model dimension. Finally, standard sharding for large models replicates the single key and value head by the number of model partitions (cite28†Pope et al., 2022 ); GQA removes the waste from such partitioning. Therefore, we expect GQA to present a particularly good trade-off for larger models.
L66: We note that GQA is not applied to the encoder self-attention layers; encoder representations are computed in parallel, and memory bandwidth is therefore generally not the primary bottleneck.
L67: ## 3 Experiments
L68: 
L69: ### 3.1 Experimental setup
L70: #### Configurations
L71: All models are based on the T5.1.1 architecture (cite31†Raffel et al., 2020 ), implemented with JAX (cite38†Bradbury et al., 2018 ), Flax (cite39†Heek et al., 2020 ), and Flaxformer^{1}^{1} 1 cite40†https://github.com/google/flaxformer†github.com . For our main experiments we consider T5 Large and XXL with multi-head attention, as well as uptrained versions of T5 XXL with multi-query and grouped-query attention.
L72: We use the Adafactor optimizer with the same hyperparameters and learning rate schedule as T5 (cite31†Raffel et al., 2020 ). We apply MQA and GQA to decoder self-attention and cross-attention, but not encoder self-attention.
L73: #### Uptraining

title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
text:
L72: We use the Adafactor optimizer with the same hyperparameters and learning rate schedule as T5 (cite31†Raffel et al., 2020 ). We apply MQA and GQA to decoder self-attention and cross-attention, but not encoder self-attention.
L73: #### Uptraining
L74: 
L75: Uptrained models are initialized from public T5.1.1 checkpoints. The key and value heads are mean-pooled to the appropriate MQA or GQA structure, and then pre-trained for a further $\alpha$ proportion of original pre-training steps with the original pre-training setup and dataset from (cite31†Raffel et al., 2020 ). For $\alpha=0.05$, training took approximately 600 TPUv3 chip-days.
L76: #### Data
L77: 
L78: We evaluate on summarization datasets CNN/Daily Mail (cite41†Nallapati et al., 2016 ), arXiv and PubMed (cite42†Cohan et al., 2018 ), MediaSum (cite43†Zhu et al., 2021 ), and Multi-News (cite44†Fabbri et al., 2019 ); translation dataset WMT 2014 English-to-German; and question answering dataset TriviaQA (cite45†Joshi et al., 2017 ). We do not evaluate on popular classification benchmarks such as GLUE (cite46†Wang et al., 2019 ) as autoregressive inference is less applicable for those tasks.
L79: #### Fine-tuning
L80: 
L81: For fine-tuning, we use a constant learning rate of 0.001, batch size 128, and dropout rate 0.1 for all tasks. CNN/Daily Mail and WMT use input length of 512 and output length 256. Other summarization datasets use input length 2048 and output length 512. Finally, TriviaQA uses input length 2048 and output length 32. We train until convergence and select the checkpoint with the highest dev performance. We use greedy decoding for inference.
L82: #### Timing
L83:

Average performance on all tasks as a function of average inference time per sample for T5-Large and T5-XXL with multi-head attention, and 5% uptrained T5-XXL with MQA and GQA-8 attention.
L95: ### 3.2 Main results
L96: Figure cite48†3 shows average performance over all datasets as a function of average inference time for MHA T5-Large and T5-XXL, and uptrained MQA and GQA-$8$ XXL models with uptraining proportion $\alpha=0.05$. We see that a larger uptrained MQA model provides a favorable trade-off relative to MHA models, with higher quality and faster inference than MHA-Large. Moreover, GQA achieves significant additional quality gains, achieving performance close to MHA-XXL with speed close to MQA.
L97: Table cite49†1 contains full results for all datasets.
L98: ### 3.3 Ablations
L99: 
L100: This section presents experiments to investigate the effect of different modeling choices. We evaluate performance on a representive subsample of tasks: CNN/Daily Mail, (short-form summarization), MultiNews (long-form summarization), and TriviaQA (question-answering).
L101: Figure 4: Performance comparison of different checkpoint conversion methods for T5-Large uptrained to MQA with proportion $\alpha=0.05$. ‘Mean’ mean-pools key and value heads, ‘First’ selects the first head and ‘Random’ initializes heads from scratch.
L102: #### Checkpoint conversion
L103: 
L104: Figure cite50†4 compares the performance of different methods for checkpoint conversion. Mean pooling appears to work best, followed by selecting a single head and then random initialization. Intuitively, results are ordered by the degree to which information is preserved from the pre-trained model.
L105: #### Uptraining steps
L106: 
L107: Figure cite51†5 shows how performance varies with uptraining proportion for T5 XXL with MQA and GQA. First, we note that GQA already achieves reasonable performance after conversion while MQA requires uptraining to be useful. Both MQA and GQA gain from 5% uptraining with diminishing returns from 10%.
L108:

title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
text:
L108: 
L109: Figure 5: Performance as a function of uptraining proportion for T5 XXL models with MQA and GQA-8.
L110: #### Number of groups
L111: 
L112: Figure cite52†6 demonstrates the effect of the number of GQA groups on inference speed. For larger models the memory bandwidth overhead from the KV cache is less constraining (cite27†Shazeer, 2019 ), while the reduction in key-value size is sharper due to the increased number of heads. As a result, increasing the number of groups from MQA only results in modest slowdowns initially, with increasing cost as we move closer to MHA. We selected 8 groups as a favorable middle ground.
L113: Figure 6: Time per sample for GQA-XXL as a function of the number of GQA groups with input length 2048 and output length 512. Going from 1 (MQA) to 8 groups adds modest inference overhead, with increasing cost to adding more groups.
L114: ## 4 Related Work
L115: This work is focused on achieving a better trade-off between decoder quality and inference time through reducing the memory bandwidth overhead (cite53†Williams et al., 2009 ) from loading keys and values. cite27†Shazeer (2019) first proposed reducing this overhead through multi-query attention. Follow-up work showed that multi-query attention is especially helpful for long inputs (cite28†Pope et al., 2022 ; cite29†de Jong et al., 2022 ). cite54†Rabe (2023) independently developed GQA with public implementation.
L116: Other works have explored grouping attention heads for computational efficiency (cite55†Park et al., 2020 ; cite56†Luo et al., 2022 ; cite57†Ni et al., 2023 ) without focusing specifically on key-value heads, which determine memory bandwidth overhead.

title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
text:
L117: A number of other methods have been proposed to reduce memory bandwidth overhead from keys and values, as well as parameters. Flash attention (cite58†Dao et al., 2022 ) structures the attention computation to avoid materializing the quadratic attention scores, reducing memory and speeding up training. Quantization (cite59†Dettmers et al., 2022 ; cite60†Frantar et al., 2022 ) reduces the size of weights and activations, including keys and values, by lowering precision.
L118: Model distillation (cite61†Hinton et al., 2015 ; cite62†Gou et al., 2021 ) instead reduces model size at a given precision, using data generated from the larger model to finetune the smaller model. Layer-sparse cross-attention (cite29†de Jong et al., 2022 ) eliminates most cross-attention layers which make up the primary expense for longer inputs.
L119: Speculative sampling (cite63†Chen et al., 2023 ; cite64†Leviathan et al., 2022 ) ameliorates the memory bandwidth bottleneck by proposing multiple tokens with a smaller model which are then scored in parallel by a larger model.
L120: Finally, the uptraining procedure we propose is inspired by cite33†Komatsuzaki et al. (2022) , which uptrains standard T5 checkpoints into sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts models.
L121: ## 5 Conclusion
L122: Language models are expensive for inference primarily due to the memory bandwidth overhead from loading keys and values. Multi-query attention reduces this overhead at the cost of decreased model capacity and quality. We propose to convert multi-head attention models to multi-query models with a small fraction of original pre-training compute.
L123: Moreover, we introduce grouped-query attention, an interpolation of multi-query and multi-head attention that achieves quality close to multi-head at comparable speed to multi-query attention.
L124: ## Limitations
L125: This paper focuses on ameliorating the memory bandwidth overhead from loading keys and values. This overhead is most important when generating longer sequences, for which quality is inherently difficult to evaluate. For summarization we employ Rouge score, which we know is a flawed evaluation that does not tell the whole story; for that reason, it is difficult to be certain our trade-offs are correct.

title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
text:
L125: This paper focuses on ameliorating the memory bandwidth overhead from loading keys and values. This overhead is most important when generating longer sequences, for which quality is inherently difficult to evaluate. For summarization we employ Rouge score, which we know is a flawed evaluation that does not tell the whole story; for that reason, it is difficult to be certain our trade-offs are correct.
L126: Due to limited computation, we also do not compare our XXL GQA model to a comparitive model trained from scratch, so we do not know the relative performance of uptraining vs training from scratch. Finally, we evaluate the impact of uptraining and GQA only on encoder-decoder models. Recently, decoder-only models are extremely popular, and since these models do not have separate self-attention and cross-attention, we expect GQA to have a stronger advantage over MQA.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L96: ## 2. Background
L97: 
L98: In this section, we describe the generation and serving procedures of typical LLMs and the iteration-level scheduling used in LLM serving.
L99: ### 2.1. Transformer-Based Large Language Models
L100: 
L101: The task of language modeling is to model the probability of a list of tokens $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}).$ Since language has a natural sequential ordering, it is common to factorize the joint probability over the whole sequence as the product of conditional probabilities (a.k.a. autoregressive decomposition (cite61†Bengio et al., 2000 )):
L102: 
L103: (1)  |  | $$P(x)=P(x_{1})\cdot P(x_{2}\mid x_{1})\cdots P(x_{n}\mid x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}).$$  |
L104: Transformers (cite50†Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have become the de facto standard architecture for modeling the probability above at a large scale. The most important component of a Transformer-based language model is its self-attention layers. For an input hidden state sequence $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, a self-attention layer first applies linear transformations on each position $i$ to get the query, key, and value vectors:
L105: (2)  |  | $$q_{i}=W_{q}x_{i},\ k_{i}=W_{k}x_{i},\ v_{i}=W_{v}x_{i}.$$  |
L106: 
L107: Then, the self-attention layer computes the attention score $a_{ij}$ by multiplying the query vector at one position with all the key vectors before it and compute the output $o_{i}$ as the weighted average over the value vectors:
L108: 
L109: (3)  |  | $$a_{ij}=\frac{\exp(q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}/\sqrt{d})}{\sum_{t=1}^{i}\exp(q_{i}^{\top}k_{t}/\sqrt{d})},\ o_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{i}a_{ij}v_{j}.$$  |

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L110: Besides the computation in Eq. cite62†4 , all other components in the Transformer model, including the embedding layer, feed-forward layer, layer normalization (cite63†Ba et al., 2016 ), residual connection (cite64†He et al., 2016 ), output logit computation, and the query, key, and value transformation in Eq. cite65†2 , are all applied independently position-wise in a form of $y_{i}=f(x_{i}).$
L111: ### 2.2. LLM Service & Autoregressive Generation
L112: 
L113: Once trained, LLMs are often deployed as a conditional generation service (e.g., completion API (cite47†OpenAI, 2020 ) or chatbot (cite45†OpenAI, 2022 ; cite46†Google, 2023 )). A request to an LLM service provides a list of input prompt tokens $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}),$ and the LLM service generates a list of output tokens $(x_{n+1},\ldots,x_{n+T})$ according to Eq. cite66†1 . We refer to the concatenation of the prompt and output lists as sequence.
L114: Due to the decomposition in Eq. cite66†1 , the LLM can only sample and generate new tokens one by one, and the generation process of each new token depends on all the previous tokens in that sequence, specifically their key and value vectors. In this sequential generation process, the key and value vectors of existing tokens are often cached for generating future tokens, known as KV cache. Note that the KV cache of one token depends on all its previous tokens.
L115: This means that the KV cache of the same token appearing at different positions in a sequence will be different.
L116: Given a request prompt, the generation computation in the LLM service can be decomposed into two phases:

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L115: This means that the KV cache of the same token appearing at different positions in a sequence will be different.
L116: Given a request prompt, the generation computation in the LLM service can be decomposed into two phases:
L117: The prompt phase takes the whole user prompt $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ as input and computes the probability of the first new token $P(x_{n+1}\mid x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$. During this process, also generates the key vectors $k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}$ and value vectors $v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}$. Since prompt tokens $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$ are all known, the computation of the prompt phase can be parallelized using matrix-matrix multiplication operations.
L118: Therefore, this phase can efficiently use the parallelism inherent in GPUs.
L119: The autoregressive generation phase generates the remaining new tokens sequentially. At iteration $t$, the model takes one token $x_{n+t}$ as input and computes the probability $P(x_{n+t+1}\mid x_{1},\ldots,x_{n+t})$ with the key vectors $k_{1},\ldots,k_{n+t}$ and value vectors $v_{1},\ldots,v_{n+t}$. Note that the key and value vectors at positions $1$ to $n+t-1$ are cached at previous iterations, only the new key and value vector $k_{n+t}$ and $v_{n+t}$ are computed at this iteration.
L120: This phase completes either when the sequence reaches a maximum length (specified by users or limited by LLMs) or when an end-of-sequence (<eos>) token is emitted. The computation at different iterations cannot be parallelized due to the data dependency and often uses matrix-vector multiplication, which is less efficient. As a result, this phase severely underutilizes GPU computation and becomes memory-bound, being responsible for most portion of the latency of a single request.
L121: Figure 3. KV cache memory management in existing systems. Three types of memory wastes – reserved, internal fragmentation, and external fragmentation – exist that prevent other requests from fitting into the memory. The token in each memory slot represents its KV cache. Note the same tokens can have different KV cache when at different positions.
L122: ### 2.3. Batching Techniques for LLMs

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L122: ### 2.3. Batching Techniques for LLMs
L123: The compute utilization in serving LLMs can be improved by batching multiple requests. Because the requests share the same model weights, the overhead of moving weights is amortized across the requests in a batch, and can be overwhelmed by the computational overhead when the batch size is sufficiently large. However, batching the requests to an LLM service is non-trivial for two reasons. First, the requests may arrive at different times.
L124: A naive batching strategy would either make earlier requests wait for later ones or delay the incoming requests until earlier ones finish, leading to significant queueing delays. Second, the requests may have vastly different input and output lengths (Fig. cite57†11 ). A straightforward batching technique would pad the inputs and outputs of the requests to equalize their lengths, wasting GPU computation and memory.
L125: To address this problem, fine-grained batching mechanisms, such as cellular batching (cite67†Gao et al., 2018 ) and iteration-level scheduling (cite52†Yu et al., 2022 ), have been proposed. Unlike traditional methods that work at the request level, these techniques operate at the iteration level. After each iteration, completed requests are removed from the batch, and new ones are added. Therefore, a new request can be processed after waiting for a single iteration, not waiting for the entire batch to complete.
L126: Moreover, with special GPU kernels, these techniques eliminate the need to pad the inputs and outputs. By reducing the queueing delay and the inefficiencies from padding, the fine-grained batching mechanisms significantly increase the throughput of LLM serving.
L127: ## 3. Memory Challenges in LLM Serving
L128: 
L129: Although fine-grained batching reduces the waste of computing and enables requests to be batched in a more flexible way, the number of requests that can be batched together is still constrained by GPU memory capacity, particularly the space allocated to store the KV cache. In other words, the serving system’s throughput is memory-bound. Overcoming this memory-bound requires addressing the following challenges in the memory management:

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L130: Large KV cache. The KV Cache size grows quickly with the number of requests. As an example, for the 13B parameter OPT model (cite59†Zhang et al., 2022 ), the KV cache of a single token demands 800 KB of space, calculated as $2$ (key and value vectors) $\times\ 5120$ (hidden state size) $\times\ 40$ (number of layers) $\times\ 2$ (bytes per FP16). Since OPT can generate sequences up to 2048 tokens, the memory required to store the KV cache of one request can be as much as 1.6 GB.
L131: Concurrent GPUs have memory capacities in the tens of GBs. Even if all available memory was allocated to KV cache, only a few tens of requests could be accommodated. Moreover, inefficient memory management can further decrease the batch size, as shown in Fig. cite58†2 . Additionally, given the current trends, the GPU’s computation speed grows faster than the memory capacity (cite68†Gholami et al., 2021 ).
L132: For example, from NVIDIA A100 to H100, The FLOPS increases by more than 2x, but the GPU memory stays at 80GB maximum. Therefore, we believe the memory will become an increasingly significant bottleneck.
L133: Complex decoding algorithms. LLM services offer a range of decoding algorithms for users to select from, each with varying implications for memory management complexity. For example, when users request multiple random samples from a single input prompt, a typical use case in program suggestion (cite43†Github, 2022 ), the KV cache of the prompt part, which accounts for 12% of the total KV cache memory in our experiment (§cite26†6.3 ), can be shared to minimize memory usage.
L134: On the other hand, the KV cache during the autoregressive generation phase should remain unshared due to the different sample results and their dependence on context and position. The extent of KV cache sharing depends on the specific decoding algorithm employed.
L135: In more sophisticated algorithms like beam search (cite69†Sutskever et al., 2014 ), different request beams can share larger portions (up to 55% memory saving, see §cite26†6.3 ) of their KV cache, and the sharing pattern evolves as the decoding process advances.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L136: Scheduling for unknown input & output lengths. The requests to an LLM service exhibit variability in their input and output lengths. This requires the memory management system to accommodate a wide range of prompt lengths. In addition, as the output length of a request grows at decoding, the memory required for its KV cache also expands and may exhaust available memory for incoming requests or ongoing generation for existing prompts.
L137: The system needs to make scheduling decisions, such as deleting or swapping out the KV cache of some requests from GPU memory.
L138: ### 3.1. Memory Management in Existing Systems
L139: Since most operators in current deep learning frameworks (cite55†Paszke et al., 2019 ; cite56†Olston et al., 2017 ) require tensors to be stored in contiguous memory, previous LLM serving systems (cite52†Yu et al., 2022 ; cite51†NVIDIA, 2023a ) also store the KV cache of one request as a contiguous tensor across the different positions.
L140: Due to the unpredictable output lengths from the LLM, they statically allocate a chunk of memory for a request based on the request’s maximum possible sequence length, irrespective of the actual input or eventual output length of the request.
L141: Fig. cite70†3 illustrates two requests: request A with 2048 maximum possible sequence length and request B with a maximum of 512. The chunk pre-allocation scheme in existing systems has three primary sources of memory wastes: reserved slots for future tokens, internal fragmentation due to over-provisioning for potential maximum sequence lengths, and external fragmentation from the memory allocator like the buddy allocator.
L142: The external fragmentation will never be used for generated tokens, which is known before serving a request. Internal fragmentation also remains unused, but this is only realized after a request has finished sampling. They are both pure memory waste. Although the reserved memory is eventually used, reserving this space for the entire request’s duration, especially when the reserved space is large, occupies the space that could otherwise be used to process other requests.
L143: We visualize the average percentage of memory wastes in our experiments in Fig. cite58†2 , revealing that the actual effective memory in previous systems can be as low as 20.4%.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L143: We visualize the average percentage of memory wastes in our experiments in Fig. cite58†2 , revealing that the actual effective memory in previous systems can be as low as 20.4%.
L144: Although compaction (cite71†Wang et al., 2022b ) has been proposed as a potential solution to fragmentation, performing compaction in a performance-sensitive LLM serving system is impractical due to the massive KV cache. Even with compaction, the pre-allocated chunk space for each request prevents memory sharing specific to decoding algorithms in existing memory management systems.
L145: ## 4. Method
L146: 
L147: cite72†Image: Refer to caption Figure 4. vLLM system overview.
L148: In this work, we develop a new attention algorithm, PagedAttention , and build an LLM serving engine, vLLM , to tackle the challenges outlined in §cite11†3 . The architecture of vLLM is shown in Fig. cite73†4 . vLLM adopts a centralized scheduler to coordinate the execution of distributed GPU workers. The KV cache manager effectively manages the KV cache in a paged fashion, enabled by PagedAttention.
L149: Specifically, the KV cache manager manages the physical KV cache memory on the GPU workers through the instructions sent by the centralized scheduler.
L150: Next, We describe the PagedAttention algorithm in §cite14†4.1 . With that, we show the design of the KV cache manager in §cite15†4.2 and how it facilitates PagedAttention in §cite16†4.3 , respectively. Then, we show how this design facilitates effective memory management for various decoding methods (§cite17†4.4 ) and handles the variable length input and output sequences (§cite18†4.5 ). Finally, we show how the system design of vLLM works in a distributed setting (§cite19†4.6 ).
L151: ### 4.1. PagedAttention

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L151: ### 4.1. PagedAttention
L152: To address the memory challenges in §cite11†3 , we introduce PagedAttention , an attention algorithm inspired by the classic idea of paging (cite74†Kilburn et al., 1962 ) in operating systems. Unlike the traditional attention algorithms, PagedAttention allows storing continuous keys and values in non-contiguous memory space. Specifically, PagedAttention partitions the KV cache of each sequence into KV blocks.
L153: Each block contains the key and value vectors for a fixed number of tokens,^{1}^{1} 1 In Transformer, each token has a set of key and value vectors across layers and attention heads within a layer. All the key and value vectors can be managed together within a single KV block, or the key and value vectors at different heads and layers can each have a separate block and be managed in separate block tables. The two designs have no performance difference and we choose the second one for easy implementation.
L154: which we denote as KV block size ($B$). Denote the key block $K_{j}=(k_{(j-1)B+1},\ldots,k_{jB})$ and value block $V_{j}=(v_{(j-1)B+1},\ldots,v_{jB}).$ The attention computation in Eq. cite62†4 can be transformed into the following block-wise computation:
L155: (4)  |  | $$A_{ij}=\frac{\exp(q_{i}^{\top}K_{j}/\sqrt{d})}{\sum_{t=1}^{\lceil i/B\rceil}\exp(q_{i}^{\top}K_{t}\mathbf{1}/\sqrt{d})},\ o_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{\lceil i/B\rceil}V_{j}A_{ij}^{\top},$$  |
L156: 
L157: where $A_{ij}=(a_{i,(j-1)B+1},\ldots,a_{i,jB})$ is the row vector of attention score on $j$-th KV block.
L158: During the attention computation, the PagedAttention kernel identifies and fetches different KV blocks separately. We show an example of PagedAttention in Fig. cite75†5 : The key and value vectors are spread across three blocks, and the three blocks are not contiguous on the physical memory.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L158: During the attention computation, the PagedAttention kernel identifies and fetches different KV blocks separately. We show an example of PagedAttention in Fig. cite75†5 : The key and value vectors are spread across three blocks, and the three blocks are not contiguous on the physical memory.
L159: At each time, the kernel multiplies the query vector $q_{i}$ of the query token (“forth”) and the key vectors $K_{j}$ in a block (e.g., key vectors of “Four score and seven” for block 0) to compute the attention score $A_{ij},$ and later multiplies $A_{ij}$ with the value vectors $V_{j}$ in a block to derive the final attention output $o_{i}.$
L160: In summary, the PagedAttention algorithm allows the KV blocks to be stored in non-contiguous physical memory, which enables more flexible paged memory management in vLLM.
L161: 
L162: Figure 5. Illustration of the PagedAttention algorithm, where the attention key and values vectors are stored as non-contiguous blocks in the memory.
L163: ### 4.2. KV Cache Manager
L164: The key idea behind vLLM’s memory manager is analogous to the virtual memory (cite74†Kilburn et al., 1962 ) in operating systems. OS partitions memory into fixed-sized pages and maps user programs’ logical pages to physical pages. Contiguous logical pages can correspond to non-contiguous physical memory pages, allowing user programs to access memory as though it were contiguous.
L165: Moreover, physical memory space needs not to be fully reserved in advance, enabling the OS to dynamically allocate physical pages as needed. vLLM uses the ideas behind virtual memory to manage the KV cache in an LLM service. Enabled by PagedAttention, we organize the KV cache as fixed-size KV blocks, like pages in virtual memory.
L166: A request’s KV cache is represented as a series of logical KV blocks, filled from left to right as new tokens and their KV cache are generated. The last KV block’s unfilled positions are reserved for future generations. On GPU workers, a block engine allocates a contiguous chunk of GPU DRAM and divides it into physical KV blocks (this is also done on CPU RAM for swapping; see §cite18†4.5 ). The KV block manager also maintains block tables—the mapping between logical and physical KV blocks of each request.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L167: Each block table entry records the corresponding physical blocks of a logical block and the number of filled positions. Separating logical and physical KV blocks allows vLLM to dynamically grow the KV cache memory without reserving it for all positions in advance, which eliminates most memory waste in existing systems, as in Fig. cite58†2 .
L168: ### 4.3. Decoding with PagedAttention and vLLM
L169: 
L170: Figure 6. Block table translation in vLLM.
L171: Next, we walk through an example, as in Fig. cite76†6 , to demonstrate how vLLM executes PagedAttention and manages the memory during the decoding process of a single input sequence: \small1⃝ As in OS’s virtual memory, vLLM does not require reserving the memory for the maximum possible generated sequence length initially. Instead, it reserves only the necessary KV blocks to accommodate the KV cache generated during prompt computation.
L172: In this case, The prompt has 7 tokens, so vLLM maps the first 2 logical KV blocks (0 and 1) to 2 physical KV blocks (7 and 1, respectively). In the prefill step, vLLM generates the KV cache of the prompts and the first output token with a conventional self-attention algorithm (e.g., (cite77†Dao et al., 2022 )). vLLM then stores the KV cache of the first 4 tokens in logical block 0 and the following 3 tokens in logical block 1. The remaining slot is reserved for the subsequent autoregressive generation phase.
L173: \small2⃝ In the first autoregressive decoding step, vLLM generates the new token with the PagedAttention algorithm on physical blocks 7 and 1. Since one slot remains available in the last logical block, the newly generated KV cache is stored there, and the block table’s #filled record is updated.
L174: \small3⃝ At the second decoding step, as the last logical block is full, vLLM stores the newly generated KV cache in a new logical block; vLLM allocates a new physical block (physical block 3) for it and stores this mapping in the block table.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L174: \small3⃝ At the second decoding step, as the last logical block is full, vLLM stores the newly generated KV cache in a new logical block; vLLM allocates a new physical block (physical block 3) for it and stores this mapping in the block table.
L175: Globally, for each decoding iteration, vLLM first selects a set of candidate sequences for batching (more in §cite18†4.5 ), and allocates the physical blocks for the newly required logical blocks. Then, vLLM concatenates all the input tokens of the current iteration (i.e., all tokens for prompt phase requests and the latest tokens for generation phase requests) as one sequence and feeds it into the LLM.
L176: During LLM’s computation, vLLM uses the PagedAttention kernel to access the previous KV cache stored in the form of logical KV blocks and saves the newly generated KV cache into the physical KV blocks. Storing multiple tokens within a KV block (block size > 1) enables the PagedAttention kernel to process the KV cache across more positions in parallel, thus increasing the hardware utilization and reducing latency. However, a larger block size also increases memory fragmentation.
L177: We study the effect of block size in §cite31†7.2 .
L178: Again, vLLM dynamically assigns new physical blocks to logical blocks as more tokens and their KV cache are generated. As all the blocks are filled from left to right and a new physical block is only allocated when all previous blocks are full, vLLM limits all the memory wastes for a request within one block, so it can effectively utilize all the memory, as shown in Fig. cite58†2 . This allows more requests to fit into memory for batching—hence improving the throughput.
L179: Once a request finishes its generation, its KV blocks can be freed to store the KV cache of other requests. In Fig. cite78†7 , we show an example of vLLM managing the memory for two sequences. The logical blocks of the two sequences are mapped to different physical blocks within the space reserved by the block engine in GPU workers.
L180: The neighboring logical blocks of both sequences do not need to be contiguous in physical GPU memory and the space of physical blocks can be effectively utilized by both sequences.
L181: Figure 7. Storing the KV cache of two requests at the same time in vLLM.
L182: ### 4.4. Application to Other Decoding Scenarios

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L180: The neighboring logical blocks of both sequences do not need to be contiguous in physical GPU memory and the space of physical blocks can be effectively utilized by both sequences.
L181: Figure 7. Storing the KV cache of two requests at the same time in vLLM.
L182: ### 4.4. Application to Other Decoding Scenarios
L183: §cite16†4.3 shows how PagedAttention and vLLM handle basic decoding algorithms, such as greedy decoding and sampling, that take one user prompt as input and generate a single output sequence. In many successful LLM applications (cite43†Github, 2022 ; cite47†OpenAI, 2020 ), an LLM service must offer more complex decoding scenarios that exhibit complex accessing patterns and more opportunities for memory sharing. We show the general applicability of vLLM on them in this section.
L184: Parallel sampling. In LLM-based program assistants (cite44†Chen et al., 2021 ; cite43†Github, 2022 ), an LLM generates multiple sampled outputs for a single input prompt; users can choose a favorite output from various candidates. So far we have implicitly assumed that a request generates a single sequence. In the remainder of this paper, we assume the more general case in which a request generates multiple sequences.
L185: In parallel sampling, one request includes multiple samples sharing the same input prompt, allowing the KV cache of the prompt to be shared as well. Via its PagedAttention and paged memory management, vLLM can realize this sharing easily and save memory.
L186: Fig. cite79†8 shows an example of parallel decoding for two outputs. Since both outputs share the same prompt, we only reserve space for one copy of the prompt’s state at the prompt phase; the logical blocks for the prompts of both sequences are mapped to the same physical blocks: the logical block 0 and 1 of both sequences are mapped to physical blocks 7 and 1, respectively. Since a single physical block can be mapped to multiple logical blocks, we introduce a reference count for each physical block.
L187: In this case, the reference counts for physical blocks 7 and 1 are both 2. At the generation phase, the two outputs sample different output tokens and need separate storage for KV cache. vLLM implements a copy-on-write mechanism at the block granularity for the physical blocks that need modification by multiple sequences, similar to the copy-on-write technique in OS virtual memory (e.g., when forking a process).

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
text:
L188: Specifically, in Fig. cite79†8 , when sample A1 needs to write to its last logical block (logical block 1), vLLM recognizes that the reference count of the corresponding physical block (physical block 1) is greater than 1; it allocates a new physical block (physical block 3), instructs the block engine to copy the information from physical block 1, and decreases the reference count to 1.
L189: Next, when sample A2 writes to physical block 1, the reference count is already reduced to 1; thus A2 directly writes its newly generated KV cache to physical block 1.
L190: In summary, vLLM enables the sharing of most of the space used to store the prompts’ KV cache across multiple output samples, with the exception of the final logical block, which is managed by a copy-on-write mechanism. By sharing physical blocks across multiple samples, memory usage can be greatly reduced, especially for long input prompts.

text:
# mygpt

A character-level GPT (3.2M parameters) used as a controlled testbed for measuring the effect of five common training/inference optimizations. Each optimization is implemented as an independent switch: the baseline and the modified run differ by exactly one flag, so any difference between them can be attributed to that single change. Every number in this document is backed by raw measurements committed under `results/*.json`.

## Results at a glance

| # | Optimization | Measured effect |
|---|---|---|
| A | LayerNorm → RMSNorm | Parameters −2,304; peak training memory 365.7 → 329.6 MB (−10%); step time unchanged |
| B | KV cache | Generation 30.5× faster at batch 32; 0.98× (no gain) at batch 1 |
| C | GQA / MQA | Per-sequence KV cache 12.0 → 6.0 → 3.0 → 1.5 MB (−87.5% for MQA) |
| D | Fused attention (SDPA) | 3.68× faster at T=2048; peak memory 607.6 → 143.6 MB |
| E | Paged KV cache | Reserved-memory waste 93.8% → 16.45%; shared prefix 2.0 → 0.25 MB |

## Purpose

The primary goal is to quantify, through controlled before/after experiments, how much each of five widely used optimizations actually improves a Transformer model, and at what cost. The emphasis is on the measurements and their interpretation rather than on building a language model or a training stack.

A secondary goal is understanding the Transformer architecture itself: causal self-attention, multi-head attention, the MLP, residual connections, normalization, and positional embeddings.

## Model and setup

```
input "F" "i" "r" "s" "t"  →  token ids (B, T)
  │
  ├─ wte  token embedding     (65 × 256)
  └─ wpe  position embedding  (128 × 256)   →  summed to (B, T, 256)
  │
  ▼   repeated 4× (each Block)
  ├─ normalization              ← A switch: LayerNorm / RMSNorm
  ├─ causal self-attention      ← B (KV cache) / C (GQA) / D (attention path)
  ├─ residual add
  ├─ normalization
  ├─ MLP  256 → 1024 → 256
  └─ residual add
  │
  ▼
  final normalization → Linear(256 → 65)  →  scores over 65 characters
                                             (weights shared with wte)
```

title: mygpt / README.md
text:
├─ residual add
  ├─ normalization
  ├─ MLP  256 → 1024 → 256
  └─ residual add
  │
  ▼
  final normalization → Linear(256 → 65)  →  scores over 65 characters
                                             (weights shared with wte)
```

Default configuration: 4 layers / 4 attention heads / 256 embedding dims / context 128 / vocab 65 (character-level). The model is trained on TinyShakespeare (≈1.1 MB).

### Parameter breakdown

| Module | Computation | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `wte` token embedding (shared with output) | 65 × 256 | 16,640 |
| `wpe` position embedding | 128 × 256 | 32,768 |
| Per layer · attention (q/k/v/c_proj) | 4 × (256×256 + 256) | 263,168 |
| Per layer · MLP | (256×1024 + 1024) + (1024×256 + 256) | 525,568 |
| Per layer · normalization ×2 | 2 × (256 + 256) | 1,024 |
| **4 blocks total** | | **3,159,040** |
| Final normalization `ln_f` | 256 + 256 | 512 |
| **Total** | | **3,208,960** |

With RMSNorm, each of the 9 normalization layers drops one bias vector → −9 × 256 = −2,304, giving 3,206,656, matching the measurement.

## Training comparison

All runs share the same configuration — 3,000 steps, batch 32, context 128, 4 layers / 4 heads / 256 dims — on a single RTX 5060 Laptop 8 GB, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu128, bf16 automatic mixed precision. Only the stated switch differs.

| run | norm | n_kv_head | params | train loss | val loss | train time | ms/step | peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `base` | LayerNorm | 4 | 3,208,960 | 1.1612 | 1.5134 | 74.2 s | 24.73 | 365.7 MB |
| `rmsnorm` | **RMSNorm** | 4 | **3,206,656** | 1.1628 | 1.5104 | 74.0 s | 24.66 | **329.6 MB** |

text:
| `rmsnorm` | **RMSNorm** | 4 | **3,206,656** | 1.1628 | 1.5104 | 74.0 s | 24.66 | **329.6 MB** |
| `gqa2` | LayerNorm | **2** | 2,945,792 | 1.1512 | 1.4994 | 83.6 s | 27.84 | 361.2 MB |
| `gqa1` | LayerNorm | **1** | 2,814,208 | 1.1614 | 1.4970 | 82.4 s | 27.44 | 359.3 MB |

A uniform random guess over 65 characters would give ln(65) ≈ 4.174; all four runs are far below this. Train and validation loss decrease together with no divergence, so 3,000 steps is well short of overfitting.

## The five optimizations

### A — RMSNorm (replacing LayerNorm)

LayerNorm subtracts the mean, divides by the standard deviation, and applies a learned scale and shift. RMSNorm ([Zhang & Sennrich, 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07467), used by the Llama family) drops the mean subtraction and the bias, keeping only the root-mean-square scaling:

```python
rms = torch.sqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + eps)
return x / rms * weight
```

**Measured**: parameters −2,304; peak training memory 365.7 → 329.6 MB (−10%); step time essentially unchanged (24.73 → 24.66 ms); val loss 1.5134 → 1.5104 (a difference of 0.003, within noise, and therefore not claimed as a quality improvement).

Step time does not change because, at this scale, each step is dominated by Python and kernel-launch overhead rather than tensor arithmetic. The measurable gain is memory.

### B — KV cache (incremental decoding)

Without a cache, every generation step recomputes the entire prefix, so the cost grows with the square of the generated length. Caching each layer's k/v reduces each step to a single new position:

```
no cache: prefix → recompute all T positions → sample 1 token     cost ∝ T²
cache:    prefix → cache k/v, then 1 position per step → sample   cost ∝ T
```

Correctness is verified before speed: with a fixed random seed, cached and uncached generation produce byte-identical text. A cache that changes the output is a bug, not an optimization; this check is part of the repository (`sample.py --use_cache`).

text:
cache:    prefix → cache k/v, then 1 position per step → sample   cost ∝ T
```

Correctness is verified before speed: with a fixed random seed, cached and uncached generation produce byte-identical text. A cache that changes the output is a bug, not an optimization; this check is part of the repository (`sample.py --use_cache`).

| batch | no cache | KV cache | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.055 s | 2.103 s | 0.98× |
| 8 | 3.566 s | 2.008 s | 1.78× |
| **32** | 88.93 s | **2.912 s** | **30.5×** |

(479 generated tokens, context 512, 4 layers / 256 dims.)

This is the plainest implementation (a `torch.cat` per step, no pre-allocated buffer, no paging); production implementations are faster still.

### C — GQA / MQA (grouped-query attention)

Standard multi-head attention (MHA) gives each query head its own key/value head, and KV cache size scales with the number of KV heads. GQA/MQA let several query heads share one key/value head.

| mode | Q heads | KV heads | sharing |
|---|---|---|---|
| MHA | 8 | 8 | one K/V per Q head |
| **GQA** | 8 | 4 / 2 | 2 or 4 Q heads share one K/V |
| MQA | 8 | 1 | all Q heads share one K/V |

KV cache size scales with the KV-head count:

| n_kv_head | mode | KV cache | vs MHA |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | MHA | 12.0 MB | 1.0× |
| 4 | GQA | 6.0 MB | 0.5× |
| 2 | GQA | 3.0 MB | 0.25× |
| 1 | MQA | 1.5 MB | 0.125× |

The figures are also verified against the actual cached tensor shapes — the KV-head dimension is reduced structurally, so the memory reduction is not merely an estimate. On this small model GQA also happens to lower validation loss (1.4970 vs 1.5134); this is a small-model artifact and must not be read as "GQA is generally better" — at real scale, GQA trades a small, controlled quality loss for memory and bandwidth. Training speed is essentially unchanged, consistent with the original paper: GQA's benefit is on the inference side, not the training side.

title: mygpt / README.md
text:
### D — Fused attention (SDPA)

The baseline materializes the full Tq × Tk score matrix before softmax; at T=2048, batch 8, 4 heads this matrix alone is `8 × 4 × 2048 × 2048`. `F.scaled_dot_product_attention` (SDPA) fuses the computation so the full matrix is never written out.

Measured on a full forward pass (batch 8, bf16, 4 layers / 4 heads / 256 dims):

| n_kv_head | impl | T=128 | T=512 | T=2048 | peak mem (T=2048) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | baseline (full matrix) | 3.73 ms | 4.63 ms | 53.91 ms | 604.3 MB |
| 4 | **fused (SDPA)** | 3.40 ms | 3.19 ms | 19.28 ms | 144.3 MB |
| 4 | chunked (online softmax) | 6.26 ms | 14.31 ms | 131.66 ms | 185.3 MB |
| 1 | baseline (full matrix) | 3.33 ms | 4.45 ms | 51.09 ms | 607.6 MB |
| 1 | **fused (SDPA)** | 3.09 ms | 3.03 ms | **13.88 ms** | **143.6 MB** |
| 1 | chunked (online softmax) | 6.12 ms | 13.65 ms | 129.37 ms | 188.6 MB |

At T=2048 the fused path is 3.68× faster (n_kv_head=1) with peak memory 607.6 → 143.6 MB. The gap grows with sequence length; at T=128 both paths are in the fixed-overhead regime and show no difference.

Three points worth noting:

- This is PyTorch's fused entry point, not the FlashAttention kernel itself. On this machine the backend that actually runs is cuDNN (`FLASH_ATTENTION` is not built, `is_flash_attention_available()` returns `False`), and the speedup holds only in bf16 — in fp32 the fused backends are mostly unavailable for grouped-query shapes.
- The default dispatcher silently selects `MATH` for grouped-query shapes (21.73 ms / 1257.3 MB); pinning the fused backend explicitly gives 1.292 ms / 41.25 MB (16.8×). The code therefore pins the backend list rather than relying on the dispatcher.

text:
- The default dispatcher silently selects `MATH` for grouped-query shapes (21.73 ms / 1257.3 MB); pinning the fused backend explicitly gives 1.292 ms / 41.25 MB (16.8×). The code therefore pins the backend list rather than relying on the dispatcher.
- A third path, `chunked` (tiling + online softmax in plain PyTorch), cuts memory (604 → 185 MB) but is slower than the baseline (53.91 → 131.66 ms). This demonstrates that the gain comes from fusing the whole computation into one kernel, not from tiling alone.

Numerical equivalence (T=64, batch 2, vs baseline): max |Δ| ≈ 6e-07 in fp32 and ≈ 1.2e-02 in bf16, argmax identical in all cases. Back-to-back runs of the same configuration vary by 1.6%–7.7%, so only gaps well beyond that are treated as results.

### E — Paged KV cache

The KV cache from improvement B stores each sequence as one contiguous tensor grown with `torch.cat`. This wastes memory in two ways: reserved allocation (a request that generates fewer tokens than its reserved maximum still holds the unused space) and duplicated prefixes (requests sharing a prompt or document each store their own copy).

Paged caching splits the cache into fixed-size blocks (16 tokens each) held in a shared pool; each sequence keeps only a block table pointing to its blocks. This enables on-demand allocation and prefix sharing via reference counting.

Capacity (4 layers / 4 heads / head dim 64 / fp16, block 16 tokens, max 512):

| requests | tokens total | reserved baseline | paged | reserved waste | paged waste |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 254 | 16.00 MB | 1.188 MB | 93.8% | 16.45% |
| 32 | 899 | 64.00 MB | 4.375 MB | 94.5% | 19.73% |

Prefix sharing (8 sequences sharing a 64-token prefix):

| | cache | prefill passes |
|---|---|---|
| one copy each | 2.000 MB | 8 |
| **paged + fork** | **0.250 MB (−87.5%)** | **1** |

Correctness: paging only changes where the same k/v is stored, so the two paths must emit byte-identical tokens (verified, `token_match = true`).

Wall-clock: this pure-Python implementation is 1.10× slower (128.68 → 141.61 ms) because each step adds a table lookup and a copy. The experiment validates capacity and sharing, not speed; real systems such as vLLM move these operations into GPU kernels and combine them with continuous batching.

## The batch-size result

The first KV-cache benchmark returned 0.98× — the cache was slower. Rather than retuning until the number looked favorable, the time was measured where it actually goes:

| seq len | 1 | 64 | 256 | 512 | 1024 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ms per forward | 10.24 | 11.50 | 11.85 | 11.59 | 13.77 |

A 1024× increase in sequence length costs only ~3.5 ms, so roughly 10 ms of every forward pass is fixed overhead (Python + kernel launches), not arithmetic. At batch 1 there is almost no GPU work to remove, so the cache cannot help. As the batch grows, the real computation appears and the cache pays off (30.5× at batch 32). The conclusion: KV cache removes arithmetic, not overhead.

## Why speculative decoding was not used

Speculative decoding accelerates a large target model by having a cheaper draft model propose several tokens and then verifying them in a single target-model pass. Its premise is that the target model's per-token cost is dominated by expensive arithmetic that the draft model can avoid.

That premise does not hold here. mygpt's per-token cost is dominated by the ~10 ms fixed overhead measured above, not by arithmetic (a 1024× increase in sequence length changes the forward time by only ~3.5 ms). A smaller draft model cannot remove this fixed overhead, and the verification step adds one more target-model forward pass on top. The theoretical speedup ceiling is about 1.4× under the most optimistic assumptions, and under sampling (the model's default mode) the result is actually slower. Speculative decoding was therefore evaluated and not implemented: at this model scale there is no arithmetic to amortize.

This is consistent with the other findings here — KV cache gives 0.98× at batch 1, SDPA is swamped at short sequences, and GQA shows no quality cost at this size — techniques whose benefit requires a much larger model or a much larger batch.

## Reproducibility

```bash
git clone https://github.com/tancy-920/mygpt.git
cd mygpt
pip install -r requirements.txt    # RTX 50 series: use the cu128 index, see the file header

python train.py --run_name base      # ~75 s on a laptop GPU
python sample.py --prompt "Shakespeare"
python bench.py                      # reproduces every inference number below
```

Reproducing the comparison experiments:

```bash
# A — RMSNorm
python train.py --run_name base    --norm layernorm
python train.py --run_name rmsnorm --norm rmsnorm

# B / C / D / E — inference side
python bench.py                     # all five benchmark groups
python bench.py 4 5                 # run only groups 4 and 5

# C — training-side quality comparison
python train.py --run_name gqa2 --n_kv_head 2
python train.py --run_name gqa1 --n_kv_head 1
```

`train.py` writes `results/<run_name>_metrics.json`; `bench.py` writes `results/bench_*.json`. The switch for improvement D (`GPTConfig.attn`) is used only on the inference-side forward comparison and is not wired into `train.py`, so training always uses the baseline path.

### Repository structure

```
mygpt/
├── model.py      GPTConfig / LayerNorm / RMSNorm / CausalSelfAttention (three attention paths) / MLP / Block / GPT
├── paged_kv.py   Paged KV cache: block pool + block table + reference counting + prefix sharing
├── train.py      Training loop + metric logging
├── sample.py     Load weights and generate (also the KV-cache equivalence check)

├── results/      Raw measurements (committed, each number here can be re-derived)

## Limitations

- This is not a usable language model: 3.2M parameters, character-level, 1.1 MB of text, 3,000 steps. It is a measurement vehicle.
- Single run, single seed, single laptop GPU. Validation-loss differences around 0.005 are noise.
- The 30.5× is not a universal constant; it is the intersection of O(T²) vs O(T) generation on this hardware at batch 32.
- The architecture is GPT-2 style (no RoPE, no SwiGLU, no gradient checkpointing). The five optimizations are introduced in isolation.
- Attention runs through PyTorch's fused entry point, not the FlashAttention kernel; the speedup is bf16-only.
- The paged KV cache is a Python-level proof of concept (no copy-on-write, no scheduler, attention still gathers blocks back into a contiguous tensor).
- The default KV cache remains the plainest `torch.cat` version; the paged path coexists in `paged_kv.py`.
- Repeated measurements vary by 1.6%–7.7%, and timing is taken on a thermally-throttling laptop.

- [karpathy/char-rnn](https://github.com/karpathy/char-rnn) — the TinyShakespeare dataset (≈1.1 MB).

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""
model.py —— 约 3.2M 参数的字符级 GPT，含四项可开关的注意力与缓存优化
======================================================================

每项改进都由配置项或调用参数控制，以便逐项做「改前 / 改后」对照实验：

    GPTConfig.norm       "layernorm" | "rmsnorm"   改进 A：RMSNorm 替换 LayerNorm
    generate(use_cache=) True | False              改进 B：KV cache 增量解码
    GPTConfig.n_kv_head  < n_head 即启用           改进 C：GQA（多个 Q 头共享一组 KV 头）
    GPTConfig.attn       "baseline" | "sdpa" | "chunked"
                                                   改进 D：注意力实现三选一
                                                   （逐位置完整矩阵 / PyTorch 融合内核 / 分块在线 softmax）

另有改进 E（分页 KV cache）不改变本文件的默认路径，见 paged_kv.py。

文件结构（自上而下 6 块）：
    GPTConfig            超参数
    LayerNorm / RMSNorm  两种归一化，改进 A 在此二选一
    CausalSelfAttention  因果自注意力，改进 B / C / D 都落在这个类里
    MLP                  前馈网络
    Block                一层 = 注意力 + MLP，各带残差与归一化
    GPT                  整体：嵌入 → N 层 Block → 输出层

命令行入口：
    train.py   训练 + 记录指标
    sample.py  加载权重生成文本
    bench.py   推理性能对照（KV cache 加速比 / GQA 显存 / 注意力实现对比 / 分页缓存容量）
"""
import math
import warnings
from dataclasses import dataclass

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.nn import functional as F

    from torch.nn.attention import SDPBackend, sdpa_kernel
except ImportError:                     # pragma: no cover
    SDPBackend = sdpa_kernel = None

class GPTConfig:

    block_size: int = 128      # 上下文长度：一次最多看 128 个字符
    vocab_size: int = 65       # 字符种类数（tinyshakespeare 为 65 种）
    n_layer: int = 4           # 堆叠多少个 Block
    n_head: int = 4            # 注意力划分为几个 Query 头
    n_kv_head: int = 4         # 改进 C：KV 头数；等于 n_head 即标准多头注意力，小于 n_head 即 GQA
    n_embd: int = 256          # 每个字符用多少维向量表示
    dropout: float = 0.0       # 小数据集设 0（更快）
    bias: bool = True          # 线性层是否带 bias
    norm: str = "layernorm"    # 改进 A 的开关："layernorm" 或 "rmsnorm"
    attn: str = "baseline"     # 改进 D 的开关："baseline" / "sdpa" / "chunked"

# ============================================================
# 因果自注意力

class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    """因果自注意力：每个位置回顾它之前的所有位置，做一次加权平均。

    q / k / v 三个投影的分工：
        q（query）当前位置在找什么信息
        k（key）  各位置有哪些特征可供匹配
        v（value）各位置能提供的具体内容
    q·k 越大代表越相关，经 softmax 归一化成权重后，用权重对 v 加权求和。

    「因果」体现在掩码上：位置 i 只能看到 j <= i，训练时不允许提前看到答案。
    改进 B（KV cache）、改进 C（GQA）、改进 D（注意力实现）都在这一个类里。

    改进 D 提供三种等价但代价不同的注意力实现，由 GPTConfig.attn 选择：
        "baseline"  逐位置算出完整的 Tq×Tk 分数矩阵，最直白，显存随 T² 增长（默认）
        "sdpa"      转交给 PyTorch 的融合注意力内核（scaled_dot_product_attention）
        "chunked"   把 key 分块、用在线 softmax 逐块累加，不生成完整的 Tq×Tk 矩阵
    """

    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        assert config.n_embd % config.n_head == 0, "n_embd 要能被 n_head 整除"
        assert config.n_head % config.n_kv_head == 0, "n_head 要能被 n_kv_head 整除（GQA 要求）"

        self.n_head = config.n_head
        self.n_kv_head = config.n_kv_head       # 改进 C：KV 头数
        self.head_dim = config.n_embd // config.n_head
        self.dropout = config.dropout
        # 改进 D：读配置决定用哪种注意力实现。旧权重文件里的 GPTConfig 可能没有这个字段，

        # 所以用 getattr 兜底，默认仍是 "baseline"（与加改进 D 之前的行为完全一致）。
        self.attn_impl = getattr(config, "attn", "baseline")
        assert self.attn_impl in ("baseline", "sdpa", "chunked"), \
            "attn 只能是 baseline / sdpa / chunked 三者之一"

        # 三个投影。nanoGPT 上游把 qkv 合并为单个 c_attn，这里拆开是为了支持 GQA（k/v 的输出维度可以更小）
        self.q_proj = nn.Linear(config.n_embd, self.n_head * self.head_dim, bias=config.bias)
        self.k_proj = nn.Linear(config.n_embd, self.n_kv_head * self.head_dim, bias=config.bias)
        self.v_proj = nn.Linear(config.n_embd, self.n_kv_head * self.head_dim, bias=config.bias)
        self.c_proj = nn.Linear(config.n_embd, config.n_embd, bias=config.bias)

        self.attn_dropout = nn.Dropout(config.dropout)
        self.resid_dropout = nn.Dropout(config.dropout)

        # 下三角掩码：第 i 行第 j 列 = 1 表示「位置 i 可以看位置 j」，仅对角线及左侧为 1
        self.register_buffer(
            "mask",
            torch.tril(torch.ones(config.block_size, config.block_size)).view(
                1, 1, config.block_size, config.block_size
            ),
        )

    def forward(self, x, past_kv=None, use_cache=False):
        """
        x       : (B, T, C)
        past_kv : 改进 B 用 —— 历史缓存 (past_k, past_v)，形状 (B, n_kv_head, 已缓存长度, head_dim)
        use_cache: 是否把本次算出的 k/v 也一并返回
        返回     : (输出 y (B,T,C), 新的 kv 缓存 或 None)
        """
        B, T, C = x.size()

        q = self.q_proj(x).view(B, T, self.n_head, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)      # (B, nh, T, hd)

        """
        B, T, C = x.size()

        q = self.q_proj(x).view(B, T, self.n_head, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)      # (B, nh, T, hd)
        k = self.k_proj(x).view(B, T, self.n_kv_head, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)   # (B, nkv, T, hd)
        v = self.v_proj(x).view(B, T, self.n_kv_head, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)

        # ---- 改进 B：KV cache ----
        # 生成时每步只喂 1 个新字符，但注意力需要「前面所有字符」的 k/v。
        # 无缓存：每次重算前面全部；有缓存：直接接上历史，只算新字符。
        if past_kv is not None:
            past_k, past_v = past_kv
            k = torch.cat((past_k, k), dim=2)
            v = torch.cat((past_v, v), dim=2)
        new_kv = (k, v) if use_cache else None

        Tq, Tk = q.size(2), k.size(2)
        # 因果掩码的切片：Tq == Tk（训练、整段前向）时取到的就是标准下三角；
        # Tq == 1（增量解码）时取的是最后一行，全为 1，表示当前字符可以看到全部历史。
        mask = self.mask[:, :, Tk - Tq : Tk, :Tk]

        # ---- 改进 D：三种实现算的是同一件事，只是做法与代价不同 ----
        if self.attn_impl == "sdpa":
            y = self._attn_sdpa(q, k, v, mask)
        elif self.attn_impl == "chunked":
            y = self._attn_chunked(q, k, v, mask)
        else:
            y = self._attn_baseline(q, k, v, mask)

        y = y.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, Tq, C)
        return self.resid_dropout(self.c_proj(y)), new_kv

    def _expand_kv(self, k, v):

    def _expand_kv(self, k, v):
        """改进 C：k/v 头数少于 q 头数时，把每个 k/v 头复制若干份，各自服务一组 q 头。

        效果：KV cache 的显存占用按 n_kv_head / n_head 缩小。
        """
        if self.n_kv_head == self.n_head:
            return k, v
        rep = self.n_head // self.n_kv_head
        return k.repeat_interleave(rep, dim=1), v.repeat_interleave(rep, dim=1)

    def _attn_baseline(self, q, k, v, mask):
        """基线实现：先把完整的 Tq×Tk 分数矩阵算出来，再 softmax、加权求和。

        最直白的做法，显存占用随 Tk 线性增长（B=8、4 头、T=2048 实测峰值 532 MiB）。
        """
        k, v = self._expand_kv(k, v)
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) * (1.0 / math.sqrt(self.head_dim))   # (B, nh, Tq, Tk)
        att = att.masked_fill(mask == 0, float("-inf"))
        att = self.attn_dropout(F.softmax(att, dim=-1))
        return att @ v                                                       # (B, nh, Tq, hd)

    def _attn_sdpa(self, q, k, v, mask):
        """交给 PyTorch 的融合注意力内核（scaled_dot_product_attention）计算。

        两个容易踩错的地方，都是实测确认过的，写在这里避免以后改错：
          1. 掩码用 bool 张量显式传入，不要用 is_causal=True。SDPA 的 is_causal 是
             「左上对齐」：Tq=1、Tk=64 时它只让当前这个 query 看到第 0 个 key，而基线实现
             允许它看到全部 64 个，两者输出相差 3.2（不是舍入误差）。显式传掩码则与基线
             实现逐元素一致（差值 2.9e-3，bf16 精度量级）。

    def _attn_chunked(self, q, k, v, mask, block=64):
        """分块 + 在线 softmax：把 key 沿长度切成若干块逐块累加，不生成完整的 Tq×Tk 矩阵。

        算法结构与 FlashAttention 相同（分块、维护 running max 与 running sum、用重缩放
        系数把上一轮的累加结果折算到新的 max 上），区别在于这里是纯 PyTorch 的逐块算子
        组合，不是编译到 GPU 的融合内核。

        代价与收益（bench.py 实验 4 有实测）：峰值显存不再随 Tk² 增长，整模型 T=2048 时
        基线 604 MB → 本实现 185 MB；代价是每个分块一次算子启动开销，墙钟比基线慢。

        一处与基线不同的细节：dropout 打在这里（加权平均之后），基线打在 softmax 之后、
        乘 v 之前。dropout=0 时两者完全等价（本仓库全部实验都是 0）；dropout>0 时两者是
        同一期望的两种采样实现，不再逐元素相等。

# 用 fp32 的最小有限值而不是 -inf 起手：若某一块被整块屏蔽，-inf 减 -inf 会得到 NaN
        m_i = torch.full((B, nh, Tq, 1), torch.finfo(torch.float32).min,
                         device=q.device, dtype=torch.float32)
        l_i = torch.zeros((B, nh, Tq, 1), device=q.device, dtype=torch.float32)

        for start in range(0, Tk, block):
            end = min(start + block, Tk)
            s = (q @ k[:, :, start:end, :].transpose(-2, -1)).float() * scale   # (B, nh, Tq, 本块长度)
            s = s.masked_fill(mask[:, :, :, start:end] == 0, float("-inf"))

            m_new = torch.maximum(m_i, s.max(dim=-1, keepdim=True).values)   # 加入本块后的最大值
            alpha = torch.exp(m_i - m_new)                                   # 旧累加结果要乘的折算系数
            p = torch.exp(s - m_new)                                         # 本块权重（已按新 max 归一化）
            l_i = l_i * alpha + p.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
            out = out * alpha + p @ v[:, :, start:end, :].float()
            m_i = m_new

        y = out / l_i                                     # 除以权重总和，得到加权平均
        return self.attn_dropout(y).to(q.dtype)


# ============================================================
# 前馈网络
# ============================================================
class MLP(nn.Module):
    """前馈网络：每个位置独立过一遍，位置之间不交换信息。维度 n_embd → 4·n_embd → n_embd。"""

    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        self.c_fc = nn.Linear(config.n_embd, 4 * config.n_embd, bias=config.bias)
        self.gelu = nn.GELU()
        self.c_proj = nn.Linear(4 * config.n_embd, config.n_embd, bias=config.bias)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(config.dropout)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.dropout(self.c_proj(self.gelu(self.c_fc(x))))

class Block(nn.Module):
    """一层 = 先自注意力（每个位置汇总前文）+ 再 MLP（各自加工）。

    `x = x + ...` 是残差连接：把输入原样加回输出，使梯度沿这条路径直接回传，
    深层网络才训得动。
    """

    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln_1 = make_norm(config, config.n_embd)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(config)
        self.ln_2 = make_norm(config, config.n_embd)
        self.mlp = MLP(config)

    def forward(self, x, past_kv=None, use_cache=False):
        attn_out, new_kv = self.attn(self.ln_1(x), past_kv=past_kv, use_cache=use_cache)
        x = x + attn_out
        x = x + self.mlp(self.ln_2(x))
        return x, new_kv

# 完整模型

class GPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__()
        self.config = config
        self.wte = nn.Embedding(config.vocab_size, config.n_embd)   # 字符编号 → 向量
        self.wpe = nn.Embedding(config.block_size, config.n_embd)   # 位置编号 → 向量
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(config.dropout)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([Block(config) for _ in range(config.n_layer)])
        self.ln_f = make_norm(config, config.n_embd)
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(config.n_embd, config.vocab_size, bias=False)

        self.apply(self._init_weights)
        # 参考 nanoGPT：对参与残差相加的投影层，按层数缩小初始化标准差，训练更稳定
        for pn, p in self.named_parameters():
            if pn.endswith("c_proj.weight"):
                torch.nn.init.normal_(p, mean=0.0, std=0.02 / math.sqrt(2 * config.n_layer))

    return n_req * 2 * n_layer * n_kv_head * max_len * head_dim * dtype_bytes

def time_generate(model, prompt, max_new_tokens, use_cache, repeats=2):
    """跑 repeats 次生成，取最快的一次（避免首次编译/预热干扰）。"""
    best = float("inf")
    for _ in range(repeats):
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        model.generate(prompt.clone(), max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens, use_cache=use_cache)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return best
